title: Is this Sharpe ratio real?
objectives: Test a strategy’s Sharpe ratio and adjust for the number of strategies tried.

screens.title: A 1.5 Sharpe over two years
screens.prose: A manager shows a Sharpe ratio of 1.5 over 2 years. Suppose she has no skill: her true Sharpe is 0. The curve is her measured Sharpe across many imagined 2-year records.

params.xLabel: Measured Sharpe ratio of a no-skill strategy

screens.question: How often would a no-skill manager measure 1.5 or more over 2 years?

options.why: You treated the measured Sharpe as precise. Over 2 years it wanders by about 0.7 either way.
That would need a spread near 2.2. Here 1.5 sits about 2.1 spreads above 0.
Half of no-skill records land above 0, not above 1.5.

hints.text: How wide is the curve? Most of it sits between about $-1.4$ and $1.4$.
The shaded tail is the share at 1.5 or more.
The spread is $1/\sqrt 2 = 0.71$, so 1.5 is 2.12 spreads above 0. $P(Z \ge 2.12) = 0.017$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge 1.5 against the width of the curve, not against 0 alone.

explain.text: Over 2 years a no-skill Sharpe has spread $1/\sqrt 2 = 0.71$. So 1.5 sits $1.5 / 0.71 = 2.12$ spreads above 0, and $P(Z \ge 2.12) = 0.017$. Rare for one manager, but common if 60 were tried.

screens.title: Longer records
screens.prose: Slide the length of the record $T$. The spread of a no-skill Sharpe shrinks as $T$ grows. The shaded tail is still 1.5 or more.

params.xLabel: Measured Sharpe ratio of a no-skill strategy

derive.caption: $T = {{T}}$ years: spread {{fixed(1 / sqrt(T), 3)}}, so 1.5 sits {{fixed(1.5 * sqrt(T), 2)}} spreads above 0

screens.question: Find the shortest record for which 1.5 sits at least 3 spreads above 0.

widget.label: Years of record
widget.accept: 4 years exactly: the spread is $1/\sqrt 4 = 0.5$, and $1.5 / 0.5 = 3$.

hints.text: Slide $T$ up and read the caption.
The caption gives how many spreads 1.5 sits above 0. Watch the shaded tail shrink.
You need a spread of $1.5 / 3 = 0.5$, so $1/\sqrt T = 0.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the caption first reads 3.00 or more.

byKey.linear: At 2 years 1.5 is only 2.12 spreads out. The spread shrinks with $\sqrt T$, not $T$.
byKey.nine: At 9 years 1.5 is 4.5 spreads out. A shorter record already reaches 3.
byKey.three: At 3 years the spread is 0.577, so 1.5 is 2.60 spreads out, short of 3.

explain.text: At $T = 4$ the spread is $1/\sqrt 4 = 0.5$, so 1.5 sits exactly 3 spreads above 0. Going from 2.12 to 3 spreads took twice the data. That square root is why track records must be long.

screens.title: The $t$ statistic of a Sharpe ratio
screens.prose: You divided the Sharpe ratio by its spread, the **standard error** $1/\sqrt T$. That gives its $t$ statistic: $$t = \frac{\mathrm{SR}}{1/\sqrt T} = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T,$$ with SR annualised and $T$ in years.

params.xLabel: Measured Sharpe ratio of a no-skill strategy

state.caption: No-skill Sharpe over 9 years: standard error $1/3$

screens.question: A strategy has a Sharpe ratio of 0.8 over 9 years. What is its $t$ statistic?

hints.text: Multiply the Sharpe ratio by $\sqrt T$.
Here $\sqrt 9 = 3$, and the curve's spread is $1/3$.

byKey.times: You multiplied by $T$. The standard error falls with $\sqrt T$, so multiply by $\sqrt 9 = 3$.
byKey.divide: You divided by $\sqrt T$. Dividing by the standard error $1/\sqrt T$ multiplies by $\sqrt T$.
byKey.divT: You divided by $T$. Multiply by $\sqrt T$ instead.

explain.text: $t = 0.8 \times \sqrt 9 = 2.4$: the Sharpe sits 2.4 standard errors above 0. A no-skill strategy does this with chance $P(Z \ge 2.4) = 0.008$. For one strategy chosen in advance, that is strong evidence.

screens.title: The best of a hundred
screens.prose: Now a researcher tries 100 strategies over 5 years. Every one has true Sharpe 0. She keeps the best. Each run below is one such search, and the bars show the best Sharpe it found.

params.xLabel: Best Sharpe among 100 noise strategies, 5 years

derive.caption: {{(ran).toLocaleString('en-GB')}} searches. screens.question: Run at least 1,000 searches. What is the average best Sharpe?

widget.label: Average best Sharpe
widget.accept: any value from 1.07 to 1.17. The exact mean is $E[\max] / \sqrt 5 = 2.508 / 2.236 = 1.12$.

hints.text: Press Run 1,000 and read the caption.
The caption averages the best Sharpe over the searches you ran. The tallest bars sit near 1.1.
It settles near 1.1.

feedback.correct: About 1.12, from strategies with no skill at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 searches and read the average in the caption.

byKey.zero: You expected noise to average 0. Each strategy does, but the best of 100 does not.
byKey.se: That is one strategy's standard error, $1/\sqrt 5$. The best of 100 sits much higher.

explain.text: The best of 100 noise strategies averages a Sharpe of about 1.12 over 5 years. Its $t$ is $1.12 \times \sqrt 5 = 2.5$, which looks significant for one test. Every one of these strategies is noise.

screens.title: A Sharpe of 1.0 from nothing
screens.prose: Same searches. A Sharpe of 1.0 over 5 years would impress most investors. How often does the best of 100 noise strategies reach it?

params.xLabel: Best Sharpe among 100 noise strategies, 5 years

derive.caption: {{(ran).toLocaleString('en-GB')}} searches. Share with best Sharpe 1.0 or more: {{fixed(total(['b10', 'b11', 'b12', 'b13', 'b14', 'b15', 'b16', 'b17', 'b18', 'b19', 'b20', 'b21', 'b22', 'b23']), 3)}}

screens.question: Run at least 1,000 searches. What share found a best Sharpe of 1.0 or more?

hints.text: Run 1,000 and read the caption.
The caption adds the bars from 1.0 upwards, starting with this one.
It settles near 0.72.

feedback.correct: About 72% of searches over pure noise reach 1.0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 searches and read the share in the caption.

byKey.one: That is the chance for one strategy, $1 - \Phi(\sqrt 5) = 0.013$. The search had 100 tries.
byKey.rest: That is the share that stayed below 1.0.

explain.text: About 72% of searches over noise find a best Sharpe of 1.0 or more. Exactly, $1 - \Phi(\sqrt 5)^{100} = 0.72$. A 1.0 that was the best of 100 is what no skill usually produces.

screens.title: Raise the bar with $N$
screens.prose: After trying $N$ strategies, the best must clear a Bonferroni bar: $t \ge z_{1 - 0.05/N}$, one-sided. Dividing by $\sqrt T$ turns that into a Sharpe. The curve is that bar for a 5-year record.

derive.caption: $N = {{p1.x}}$: the best needs a Sharpe of {{fixed(p1.y, 2)}} over 5 years

screens.question: Set $N = 50$. What Sharpe must the best of 50 clear? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Sharpe the best of 50 must clear

hints.text: Slide $N$ to 50 and read the caption.

feedback.correct: 1.38 over 5 years for the best of 50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption at $N = 50$, or compute $3.09 / \sqrt 5$.

byKey.one: That is the bar for one strategy, $1.645 / \sqrt 5$. Set $N = 50$.
byKey.t: That is the bar on $t$. Divide by $\sqrt 5$ to turn it into a Sharpe ratio.
byKey.rule: That is the bar for 20 strategies. Set $N = 50$.

explain.text: For $N = 50$ the bar is $z_{0.999} / \sqrt 5 = 3.09 / 2.236 = 1.38$. With one strategy it was $1.645 / 2.236 = 0.74$. Raising the bar with every strategy tried is the idea behind haircut and deflated Sharpe ratios.

screens.title: The best of fifty
screens.prose: A manager reports a Sharpe of 1.5 over 2 years, so $t = 1.5\sqrt 2 = 2.12$. Later you learn it was the best of 50 strategies she ran. The curve is the bar for a 2-year record.
screens.question: Is her record evidence of skill?

options.why: You used the bar for one test. She ran 50, so the best must clear $z_{0.999} = 3.09$.

options.text: No: the best of 50 over 2 years must clear a Sharpe of about 2.19
Yes: a Sharpe of 1.5 is high for any fund
options.why: You judged the size, not the noise. Over 2 years the standard error is 0.71, so 1.5 is only 2.1 errors from 0.

options.text: No: a Sharpe ratio cannot be tested
options.why: It can: $t = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T$. This one simply fails the bar for 50 tries.

hints.text: How many strategies did she try?
The marked point is the bar for $N = 50$; her 1.5 is the dashed line.

feedback.correct: 1.5 is well short of the 2.19 bar for the best of 50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare her 1.5 with the bar for 50 strategies over 2 years.

byKey.one-test: You used the bar for one test. She ran 50, so the best must clear $z_{0.999} = 3.09$, a Sharpe of 2.19.

explain.text: Over 2 years the bar for the best of 50 is $3.09 / \sqrt 2 = 2.19$, well above her 1.5. Even alone, 1.5 has standard error 0.71 and only $t = 2.12$. Two years and 50 tries cannot tell skill from luck.

screens.title: One rule, 25 years
screens.prose: Edge case. A pension fund fixed one rule in advance and has run it, unchanged, for 25 years. Nothing else was tried, so $N = 1$. Its Sharpe ratio is 0.5.

params.xLabel: Measured Sharpe ratio of a no-skill strategy

state.caption: No-skill Sharpe over 25 years: standard error 0.2

screens.question: What is its $t$ statistic?

hints.text: Use $t = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the Sharpe by $\sqrt{25}$.

byKey.times: You multiplied by $T$. Multiply by $\sqrt T = 5$.
byKey.divide: You divided by $\sqrt T$. Multiply by it.

explain.text: $t = 0.5 \times \sqrt{25} = 2.5$, and with $N = 1$ there is no bar to raise: one-sided $p = 0.006$. A modest Sharpe on a long, single, pre-set record is real evidence. Length and honesty about $N$ matter more than size.

screens.title: Why the best grows so slowly
screens.prose: Let $Z_1, \dots, Z_N$ be the $t$ statistics of $N$ noise strategies, each close to a standard normal. How large is their maximum likely to be?
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $P(\max_i Z_i > x) = P(\text{some } Z_i > x)$, since the max passes $x$ exactly when one $Z_i$ does
$\le N \, P(Z > x)$, by the union bound
$\le N e^{-x^2/2}$, since a standard normal tail is at most $e^{-x^2/2}$ for $x \ge 0$
The bound falls below 1 once $x > \sqrt{2 \ln N}$, so the max seldom goes far past it
Best noise Sharpe $\approx \sqrt{2 \ln N} / \sqrt T$, dividing $t$ by $\sqrt T$

hints.text: Start by turning the maximum into an event about some $Z_i$.
The union bound comes before the normal tail.
Event, union bound, tail bound, solve for $x$, then divide by $\sqrt T$.

feedback.correct: A union bound and a tail bound give $\sqrt{2 \ln N}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound the chance first, then solve for where the bound reaches 1.

byKey.tail: The tail bound applies to each term, so the union bound must come first.
byKey.solve: Solving needs the bound $N e^{-x^2/2}$ first.

explain.text: The bound says the max of $N$ noise $t$ statistics seldom passes $\sqrt{2\ln N}$: 3.03 for $N = 100$. Its actual mean is lower, 2.51, so the rule is a generous bar. Over 5 years it gives $3.03/\sqrt 5 = 1.36$, against the 1.12 your searches found.

screens.title: The flagship fund
screens.prose: A fund markets a 3-year Sharpe ratio of 1.2. Its parent firm ran 30 internal strategies over those 3 years and launched the best. The curve is the rule of thumb for the best of $N$ noise strategies.
screens.question: By the rule of thumb, what Sharpe would the best of 30 noise strategies reach over 3 years? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Best noise Sharpe of 30 over 3 years

hints.text: Use $\sqrt{2 \ln N} / \sqrt T$ with $N = 30$ and $T = 3$.
$\sqrt{6.802} = 2.608$, then divide by $\sqrt 3 = 1.732$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\sqrt{2 \ln 30}$, then divide by $\sqrt 3$.

byKey.nosqrt: That is $\sqrt{2 \ln 30}$, a $t$ statistic. Divide by $\sqrt 3$ for a Sharpe ratio.
byKey.se: That is one strategy's standard error, $1/\sqrt 3$.
byKey.fund: That is the fund's own figure. The question asks what noise alone would give.

explain.text: $\sqrt{2 \ln 30} / \sqrt 3 = 2.608 / 1.732 = 1.51$. A simulation gives a mean best of 1.18. So 1.2 is just what the best of 30 noise strategies looks like. The marketed number is not evidence of skill.

screens.title: How long a record?
screens.prose: Same fund, best of 30. To pass a Bonferroni bar, its $t$ must clear $z_{1 - 0.05/30} = 2.94$. Suppose its Sharpe stays at 1.2.

params.yLabel: Sharpe the best of 30 must clear

screens.question: How many years of record would a Sharpe of 1.2 need to clear the bar? Give 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Solve $1.2\sqrt T = 2.94$.
The record is long enough where the curve meets the dashed line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $1.2 \sqrt T = 2.94$ for $T$.

byKey.nosquare: That is $\sqrt T$. Square it to get $T$.
byKey.one-test: That uses the one-test bar, 1.645. The fund was the best of 30.

explain.text: Solve $1.2\sqrt T = 2.94$: $T = (2.94 / 1.2)^2 = 6.0$ years. Even a fund whose true Sharpe is 1.2 clears that bar only about half the time after 6 years. Ask for the number of strategies tried and the record length together.

ideas: A Sharpe ratio over $T$ years has standard error about $1/\sqrt T$, so $t = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T$: 1.5 over 2 years is only $t = 2.12$.
The best of $N$ noise strategies has a Sharpe near $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$, or a little below: about 1.1 for 100 strategies over 5 years.
Raise the bar with $N$: the best must clear $z_{1-\alpha/N}/\sqrt T$. One pre-set strategy with a long record needs no haircut.

formula.name: t statistic of a Sharpe ratio
formula.note: SR annualised, $T$ in years. The standard error $1/\sqrt T$ holds for modest Sharpe ratios.

summary.trap: A high Sharpe over a short record, chosen as the best of many, is what luck usually produces.

quiz.prose: A strategy has a 4-year track record.
quiz.question: What is the standard error of its annualised Sharpe ratio?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The standard error is $1/\sqrt T$.

byKey.two: That is $\sqrt T$. Take its reciprocal.

explain.text: The standard error is $1/\sqrt T = 1/2 = 0.5$. So a measured Sharpe of 1.0 over 4 years is only 2 standard errors from 0.

quiz.prose: A strategy shows a Sharpe of 1.0 over 4 years, so $t = 2.0$. It was the best of 20 tried. The one-sided Bonferroni bar for 20 is $z_{0.9975} = 2.81$.
quiz.question: What do you conclude?

options.why: You used the one-test bar. It was the best of 20, so it must clear 2.81.

options.text: Significant: a Sharpe of 1.0 is large
options.why: Size alone is not evidence. Over 4 years the standard error is 0.5.

options.text: Significant once the Sharpe is doubled for 4 years
options.why: There is no doubling rule. Compare $t$ with the corrected bar.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $t$ with the bar for the best of 20.

explain.text: The best of 20 needs $t \ge 2.81$, a Sharpe of $2.81 / 2 = 1.40$ over 4 years. At 1.0 it falls short. The same record from one strategy fixed in advance would pass at 1.645.

quiz.prose: Use the rule of thumb $\sqrt{2 \ln N} / \sqrt T$.
quiz.question: Roughly what Sharpe does the best of 50 noise strategies reach over 4 years? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\sqrt{2 \ln 50}$, then divide by $\sqrt 4$.

byKey.nosqrt: That is the $t$ value. Divide by $\sqrt 4 = 2$.
byKey.T: You divided by $T = 4$. Divide by $\sqrt T = 2$.

explain.text: $2 \ln 50 = 7.824$, whose square root is 2.797. Dividing by $\sqrt 4 = 2$ gives 1.40. The true mean best is a little lower, $2.249 / 2 = 1.12$.

quiz.prose: Three records, each with its one-sided Bonferroni bar on $t$.
quiz.question: Which record is evidence of skill?

options.text: Sharpe 0.6 over 16 years, one rule fixed in advance: $t = 2.4$, bar 1.645
Sharpe 2.0 over 1 year, best of 10: $t = 2.0$, bar 2.58
options.why: You were drawn by the big Sharpe. Its $t$ of 2.0 misses the bar of 2.58 for 10 tries.

options.text: Sharpe 1.5 over 2 years, best of 5: $t = 2.12$, bar 2.33
options.why: $t = 2.12$ misses the bar of 2.33 for 5 tries.

feedback.correct: Only the 16-year, single-rule record clears its bar.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each $t$ with its own bar.

explain.text: Only the first record clears its bar: $0.6 \times 4 = 2.4 > 1.645$. The other two have bigger Sharpe ratios but short records and several tries. Each falls below its corrected bar.
